Electronegativity should show a steady, continuous rise with no dips or peaks, as attraction for bonding electrons gets stronger.

walkthrough:
**Recall what electronegativity does across Period 3**

Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract a pair of electrons in a covalent bond. Across Na to Cl, proton number increases while electrons add to the same shell, so nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases. That means attraction gets stronger, so electronegativity increases steadily.

**Check the shape each graph shows**

Graph A peaks sharply at $\text{Si}$ then falls, that is the melting point trend. Graph B falls continuously, that is atomic radius. Graph C goes up overall but dips at $\text{Al}$ and at $\text{S}$, that is the classic first ionisation energy pattern.

**Pick the smooth increase**

Only one graph shows a smooth, continuous increase from $\text{Na}$ (lowest) to $\text{Cl}$ (highest) with no peaks or dips. That matches the electronegativity trend perfectly, so that graph must have electronegativity on the y-axis.

options.A: Incorrect. Graph A peaks at Si then drops sharply to P. This is the melting point trend, giant covalent Si has the highest melting point, not electronegativity which never peaks in the middle.
options.B: Incorrect. Graph B shows a steady decrease from Na to Cl. This is atomic radius, which shrinks across the period due to increasing nuclear charge, the opposite of electronegativity.
options.C: Incorrect. Graph C rises overall but has two small dips at Al and S. That is first ionisation energy, where Mg > Al due to the 3p electron and P > S due to spin-pair repulsion. Electronegativity has no such dips.
options.D: Correct. Graph D shows a smooth, continuous increase from Na to Cl. This fits electronegativity perfectly, as increasing nuclear charge and decreasing radius across Period 3 give a steadily stronger pull on bonding electrons, highest at Cl.
